x-e-m1-01.title: Will Ben come to the party? Examining the hidden meaning of his answers
x-e-m1-01.goal: Split Ben's answers in the dialogue line by line, separate what has been settled from what remains, and make a judgment without asserting 'he will come' or 'he won't come.'
x-e-m1-01.material:
A dialogue between Jisu and Ben (written as text only, without pictures):

Jisu: Do you want to come to my birthday party on Saturday?
Ben: Saturday? Hmm. I have a soccer game in the morning.
Jisu: The party is at 4 p.m.
Ben: Oh, that might work. I'll probably be tired, though.
Jisu: So... are you coming?
Ben: Let me check with my mom first.
x-e-m1-01.thinking.0: Making a judgment by putting together clues from several lines
x-e-m1-01.thinking.1: Telling possibility expressions such as 'might' and 'probably' apart
x-e-m1-01.thinking.2: Splitting settled problems from remaining problems
x-e-m1-01.prereq.0: Meanings of easy expressions such as might, probably, and check with
x-e-m1-01.s.s1.prompt: Read the dialogue to the end and choose the most appropriate judgment about whether Ben will come to the party.
x-e-m1-01.s.s1.hint.0: Split Ben's words into four pieces: 'soccer game,' 'party time,' 'tired,' and 'mom.'
x-e-m1-01.s.s1.hint.1: Put the soccer game time and the party time side by side and compare whether they overlap.
x-e-m1-01.s.s1.r.a: 'Might' only expresses a possibility. Look back and check whether you read what Ben said after that.
x-e-m1-01.s.s1.r.b: This is a judgment that separates what happened to the time problem from the thing that is still left.
x-e-m1-01.s.s1.r.c: The soccer game is in the morning and the party is at 4 p.m. Compare the two times side by side.
x-e-m1-01.s.s1.r.d: 'Tired' is a worry Ben added himself. Think about whether you can read that alone as a refusal.
x-e-m1-01.s.s1.explain: The soccer game is in the morning and the party is at 4 p.m., so the times do not overlap. Ben only said he might be tired, and at the end he said he would check with his mom first. So there is something settled (the time) and something left (his mom's permission), and it is not yet decided.
x-e-m1-01.s.s2.prompt: Write two or three sentences in Korean giving the reasons for the judgment above. Quote at least one of Ben's English expressions, and say what has been settled and what remains.
x-e-m1-01.s.s2.hint.0: First write one settled thing along with its time.
x-e-m1-01.s.s2.hint.1: Then find what remains in Ben's last words and write it.
x-e-m1-01.s.s2.selfAssess.0: Did you mention both the time evidence and what remains?
x-e-m1-01.s.s2.selfAssess.1: Did you quote Ben's English expressions as evidence?
x-e-m1-01.s.s2.selfAssess.2: Did you avoid asserting 'he will come/he won't come'?
x-e-m1-01.s.s2.model.0: The soccer game is in the morning and the party is at 4 p.m., so the times do not overlap. But Ben said 'Let me check with my mom first.', so his mom's permission remains, and I judged that we do not know yet.
x-e-m1-01.s.s2.model.1: 'That might work' means it is possible, and a morning game and a 4 p.m. party do not overlap. Being tired is just a worry, and since he said at the end he would check with his mom, the decision depends on his mom's answer.
x-e-m1-01.s.s2.modelNote.1: A good answer that evaluated being tired separately.

x-e-m1-02.title: Does 'That's fine.' really mean it's okay?
x-e-m1-02.goal: Reading a little more of the dialogue at a time, form a judgment about the speaker's inner feelings, and revise your earlier judgment when a new clue appears.
x-e-m1-02.material: Sam and Dad talk about plans for Friday. The dialogue is revealed in three parts. It is written as text only, without pictures.
x-e-m1-02.thinking.0: Revising a judgment to fit new clues
x-e-m1-02.thinking.1: Using tone expressions ('…' and 'Fine?' in place of commas) as clues
x-e-m1-02.thinking.2: Separating the surface meaning from the hidden meaning
x-e-m1-02.prereq.0: Easy words such as fine, tickets, and birthday party
x-e-m1-02.prereq.1: The tone of a dialogue (…, ?) can be a clue to feelings
x-e-m1-02.s.s1.prompt: Read the dialogue one piece at a time, and each time choose your judgment about Sam's feelings.
x-e-m1-02.s.s1.hint.0: Find one new tone or word in this piece.
x-e-m1-02.s.s1.hint.1: Check one by one whether your earlier judgment fits the new piece.
x-e-m1-02.s.s1.st.0.ask: What is the most reasonable judgment about Sam's feelings from this dialogue alone?
x-e-m1-02.s.s1.st.0.after: You cannot decide from one line. 'Fine' may truly mean it's okay, or it may be said reluctantly.
x-e-m1-02.s.s1.st.0.o.a: He seems happy, but it is not certain.
x-e-m1-02.s.s1.st.0.r.a: 'Fine' can mean good, so this is a possible reading. Also look at tone such as 'Oh.' and '...'.
x-e-m1-02.s.s1.st.0.o.b: He is extremely angry with Dad.
x-e-m1-02.s.s1.st.0.r.b: There are no words or expressions yet that say he is angry. Deciding on a strong emotion from a short answer lacks evidence.
x-e-m1-02.s.s1.st.0.o.c: He says thank you, but something may be bothering him.
x-e-m1-02.s.s1.st.0.r.c: You took 'Oh.' and '...' as clues. It is only one line, so you cannot be sure.
x-e-m1-02.s.s1.st.1.ask: Read the new clue and judge again what Sam really wants.
x-e-m1-02.s.s1.st.1.after: Reading that Sam had a party plan and the tickets looked expensive, so it was hard to say, fits the new clue best. If you first judged 'he is angry,' you should revise it here.
x-e-m1-02.s.s1.st.1.o.a: He doesn't like concerts, so he answered bluntly on purpose.
x-e-m1-02.s.s1.st.1.r.a: Sam did not say he dislikes the concert. Think about why the party came up.
x-e-m1-02.s.s1.st.1.o.b: He is blaming Dad because the tickets are expensive.
x-e-m1-02.s.s1.st.1.r.b: 'Look expensive' can also be read as worry about Dad's feelings. Look for a clue about whether the tone is blaming.
x-e-m1-02.s.s1.st.1.o.c: He wants to go to the party but couldn't say so because Dad might be hurt.
x-e-m1-02.s.s1.st.1.r.c: This is a judgment that uses the two clues, the party plan and the expensive tickets, together.
x-e-m1-02.s.s1.st.2.ask: After reading to the end, how would you revise your reading of the first 'That's... fine.'?
x-e-m1-02.s.s1.st.2.after: The party ends at 6 and the concert starts at 7:30, so he can go to both. You can revise your reading: the first 'fine' had a surface meaning and a hidden meaning that differed.
x-e-m1-02.s.s1.st.2.o.a: 'Fine' was a sign of a problem, and now that problem is solved.
x-e-m1-02.s.s1.st.2.r.a: You read the first tone and the final reaction together.
x-e-m1-02.s.s1.st.2.o.b: There was no problem from the start, and 'fine' was sincere as it was.
x-e-m1-02.s.s1.st.2.r.b: If there had been no problem, Dad would not have said 'You don't sound happy.' and Sam would not have brought up the party.
x-e-m1-02.s.s1.st.2.o.c: The problem went away because Dad canceled the concert.
x-e-m1-02.s.s1.st.2.r.c: The concert was not canceled. Read the two times, 7:30 and 6:00, again.
x-e-m1-02.s.s1.reflect: While reading the three pieces, was there a place where your judgment about Sam's feelings changed? If it did, think of one thing that was said that caused it.
x-e-m1-02.s.s2.prompt: Choose the line where the first tone clue appears that Sam's 'That's... fine.' may not be real happiness.
x-e-m1-02.s.s2.hint.0: In the line Sam said first, look for symbols or short sounds used besides words.
x-e-m1-02.s.s2.hint.1: Which line comes before Dad says 'You don't sound happy.'?
x-e-m1-02.s.s2.explain: In line 2, Sam says 'fine' using 'Oh.' and '...'. The tone shows hesitation. Line 3 is where Dad notices that tone, and line 4 is where the reason is directly revealed.

x-e-m1-03.title: A class photo notice for an absent friend: fixing what was copied wrongly
x-e-m1-03.goal: In a summary copied from a notice, find the line that differs from the notice, and fix it with one English sentence.

A school notice (written as text only, without pictures):

Notice to Grade 7 Students
Class Photo Day
Date: Thursday, May 9
Time: 8:40 a.m. - 9:10 a.m.
Place: School gym
Please wear your school uniform for the photo. If it rains, the photo will be taken in your classroom. Also bring your PE clothes for the afternoon class.

There is a message that a classmate summarized and sent to an absent friend.
x-e-m1-03.thinking.0: Checking the original against the summary line by line
x-e-m1-03.thinking.1: Telling apart two items that look alike
x-e-m1-03.thinking.2: Verifying that the corrected sentence matches the original
x-e-m1-03.prereq.0: Easy words such as uniform, PE clothes, and afternoon
x-e-m1-03.s.s1.prompt: Choose the one line in the summary message that does not match the notice.
x-e-m1-03.s.s1.hint.0: Find which line of the notice each line of the summary came from, and connect them with lines.
x-e-m1-03.s.s1.hint.1: Count how many times the notice mentions clothes.
x-e-m1-03.s.s1.explain: Line 3 does not match. The notice says to wear the school uniform for the photo and to bring PE clothes for the afternoon class. Lines 1, 2 and 4 match the notice.
x-e-m1-03.s.s2.prompt: Fix the wrong line with one or two English sentences. Make it match the notice, and make sure what to wear for the photo and what to bring for the afternoon class are not confused.
x-e-m1-03.s.s2.hint.0: First write in one sentence what to wear when the photo is taken.
x-e-m1-03.s.s2.hint.1: Find when the PE clothes are needed in the notice and add it, or check whether the PE clothes are not needed.
x-e-m1-03.s.s2.selfAssess.0: Can you say which line of the notice your corrected sentence matches?
x-e-m1-03.s.s2.selfAssess.1: Did you decide whether it is okay to leave out the PE clothes entirely, or to connect them to the afternoon class?
x-e-m1-03.s.s2.selfAssess.2: Is your English sentence a complete sentence?
x-e-m1-03.s.s2.modelNote.1: A short answer that connects the PE clothes to the afternoon.

x-e-m1-04.title: A camp application email: choosing what to ask about that is not on the poster
x-e-m1-04.goal: Separate the information already on the poster from what is missing, and politely ask in an English email only about what is truly needed in your situation but missing.
x-e-m1-04.material:
A Saturday English camp poster (written as text only, without pictures):

Saturday English Camp
For grade 7-9 students
10:00 a.m. - 3:00 p.m.
Place: City Library, Room 2
Fee: 5,000 won
To join, send an email to Ms. Park.

Haeun (grade 7) wants to join. But her Saturday morning swimming class ends at 10, and it takes 20 minutes to walk from the pool to the library. The camp runs until 3, so lunchtime falls in the middle, and the poster says nothing about lunch.
x-e-m1-04.thinking.0: Separating information already given from missing information
x-e-m1-04.thinking.1: Choosing the questions needed in my situation
x-e-m1-04.prereq.0: Polite questions such as Could I ...? and Can I ...?
x-e-m1-04.prereq.1: Comparing the poster's times with my schedule
x-e-m1-04.s.s1.prompt: Choose everything Haeun should ask Ms. Park by email. Do not choose questions the poster already answers.
x-e-m1-04.s.s1.hint.0: Cross out the information already on the poster, one item at a time.
x-e-m1-04.s.s1.hint.1: Among the remaining questions, find the ones connected to Haeun's swimming class time or lunchtime.
x-e-m1-04.s.s1.r.a: The grade is on the second line of the poster. Did you check whether the answer to the question can be found on the poster?
x-e-m1-04.s.s1.r.b: This question was chosen by comparing the time Haeun's swimming class ends and the time it takes to get to the library with the poster's start time.
x-e-m1-04.s.s1.r.c: The fee is written on the poster. It is a question that already has an answer.
x-e-m1-04.s.s1.r.d: This question was chosen by connecting the fact that the camp lasts until 3 and the fact that the poster does not mention lunch.
x-e-m1-04.s.s1.r.e: The place is written on the poster. It is a question that already has an answer.
x-e-m1-04.s.s1.explain: The poster has the grade (7-9), time, place and fee. What Haeun needs but the poster lacks are 'whether it is okay to arrive late' (arriving around 10:20 after swimming) and 'whether to bring lunch.'
x-e-m1-04.s.s2.prompt: Write an email to Ms. Park in English, 2 to 4 sentences. Politely include a greeting, a line saying you want to join, and the two questions you chose above.
x-e-m1-04.s.s2.hint.0: First write the greeting and the sentence saying you want to join.
x-e-m1-04.s.s2.hint.1: Write each question as one sentence in a pattern like Could I ...? or Do I ...?
x-e-m1-04.s.s2.selfAssess.0: Do both questions come from Haeun's situation?
x-e-m1-04.s.s2.selfAssess.1: Did you avoid asking again about what is already on the poster?
x-e-m1-04.s.s2.selfAssess.2: Does it have a greeting and a closing?
x-e-m1-04.s.s2.modelNote.1: A short answer that asks only the two questions without giving the swimming reason.

x-e-m1-05.title: A neighbor's note: what do they really want to say?
x-e-m1-05.goal: Find the real purpose of a note hidden inside compliments and greetings, and explain with evidence why it was put indirectly.
x-e-m1-05.material:
A note the downstairs neighbor stuck on the upstairs front door (written as text only, without pictures):

Hello! I'm Tom Lee from apartment 302, below you. I love music too, and your piano sounds great! By the way, my baby goes to bed at 9 p.m., and she sleeps very lightly. Thank you!
x-e-m1-05.thinking.0: Sorting what each sentence does (greeting, compliment, request)
x-e-m1-05.thinking.1: Finding the main content after by the way
x-e-m1-05.thinking.2: Evaluating the reason for putting something indirectly
x-e-m1-05.prereq.0: That By the way is used to bring up a new topic
x-e-m1-05.prereq.1: The meaning of sleep lightly (to be a light sleeper)
x-e-m1-05.s.s1.prompt: What is the most important purpose for which Tom Lee wrote this note?
x-e-m1-05.s.s1.hint.0: Name what each sentence does: 'greeting,' 'compliment,' or 'another topic.'
x-e-m1-05.s.s1.hint.1: Think about how what comes after By the way connects to the earlier compliment.
x-e-m1-05.s.s1.o.a: To compliment the neighbor on their wonderful piano playing
x-e-m1-05.s.s1.r.a: The compliment is in the note, but compare it with what comes after By the way to see whether the note is only meant to compliment.
x-e-m1-05.s.s1.o.b: To try asking for music recommendations that the baby might like
x-e-m1-05.s.s1.r.b: The baby is mentioned, but look in the note for whether it asks for music recommendations.
x-e-m1-05.s.s1.o.c: To gently ask them to lower the sound after 9 o'clock
x-e-m1-05.s.s1.r.c: This is a judgment that separated what the note's three parts (greeting, compliment, talk about the baby) do.
x-e-m1-05.s.s1.o.d: To tell the person upstairs where they live and say hello
x-e-m1-05.s.s1.r.d: The self-introduction is in the first sentence, but consider whether that is the note's most important purpose.
x-e-m1-05.s.s1.explain: The note starts with a greeting and a compliment and then, with 'By the way,' brings up that the baby sleeps at 9 and sleeps lightly. It does not directly write 'please be quiet,' but it can be read as a note asking them to lower the sound after 9 p.m.
x-e-m1-05.s.s2.prompt: Write two or three sentences in Korean about why Tom Lee did not write the request directly and put it this indirect way. Quote at least one English expression from the note as evidence.
x-e-m1-05.s.s2.hint.0: Find one English expression in the note that reads like a request.
x-e-m1-05.s.s2.hint.1: Think about how that expression would affect the neighbor's feelings.
x-e-m1-05.s.s2.selfAssess.0: Did you quote one English piece of evidence from the note?
x-e-m1-05.s.s2.selfAssess.1: Did you explain the reason for the indirectness from the neighbor's point of view?
x-e-m1-05.s.s2.selfAssess.2: Did you clearly state the purpose, 'a request'?
x-e-m1-05.s.s2.model.0: By giving the reason with 'my baby goes to bed at 9 p.m.,' he made the request gently without hurting the neighbor's feelings.
x-e-m1-05.s.s2.model.1: Saying 'be quiet' directly could sound rude, so he complimented first and then mentioned that the baby sleeps at 9, letting the neighbor realize it on their own.
x-e-m1-05.s.s2.modelNote.1: An answer that also explained the role of the compliment.

x-e-m1-06.prereq.1: How to use need for (need ... for)

x-e-m1-06.s.s1.hint.0: For each message, say in one sentence what Jun has to do.
x-e-m1-06.s.s1.hint.1: Which message makes it hard to say what Jun has to do?

It asks whether the book was fun and talks about the weather, so it is hard for Jun to know what to do. x-e-m1-06.s.s2.hint.0: Try starting with a request pattern (Could you ...? / Can I ...?).
x-e-m1-06.s.s2.hint.1: Include an expression that gives a time or reason, such as 'need ... for,' 'by Friday,' or 'tomorrow.'
x-e-m1-06.s.s2.selfAssess.0: Is it clear what Jun has to do?
x-e-m1-06.s.s2.selfAssess.1: Did you include the reason it's needed or the time?

x-e-m1-06.title: A message to get back something you lent: choose one with a clear purpose and write your own

x-e-m1-07.title: A poster and the latest notice: which one should you follow?
x-e-m1-07.goal: Pick out exactly what differs between two sources, judge which one to trust with reasons, and tell a friend about the contradiction in English.
x-e-m1-07.material:
Source A: Poster (put up on April 28)

Student Council Movie Night
Friday, May 16, 6:30 p.m.
Room 101
Free! Bring a snack.

Source B: Notice from the same student council (posted on May 13)

Update: Movie Night will be on Saturday, May 17, at 6:30 p.m. in the gym, because Room 101 is closed for painting. See you there!
x-e-m1-07.thinking.0: Comparing the same items across two sources
x-e-m1-07.thinking.1: Separating what differs from what is not mentioned
x-e-m1-07.thinking.2: Judging trust by the date and the source of the sources
x-e-m1-07.prereq.1: Easy words such as notice and update
x-e-m1-07.s.s1.prompt: Choose all the items that the two sources say differently.
x-e-m1-07.s.s1.hint.0: For each item (date, time, place, price), write what you found in A and B side by side.
x-e-m1-07.s.s1.hint.1: Separate items that appear in only one source from items that appear in both but differ.
x-e-m1-07.s.s1.r.a: The poster says Friday and the notice says Saturday. Compare the dates of the two sources side by side.
x-e-m1-07.s.s1.r.b: Read the times of the two sources side by side. If the times are the same, it is not a contradiction.
x-e-m1-07.s.s1.r.c: The poster says Room 101 and the notice says the gym. Compare the places of the two sources side by side.
x-e-m1-07.s.s1.r.d: The notice said nothing about the price. Are saying nothing and saying something different the same?
x-e-m1-07.s.s1.explain: The date (Friday vs Saturday) and the place (Room 101 vs the gym) differ. The time is 6:30 p.m. in both, so it is the same. Only the poster said 'Free' about the price and the notice said nothing, so you cannot say they differ.
x-e-m1-07.s.s2.prompt: Which source should you follow? Choose the most appropriate judgment.
x-e-m1-07.s.s2.hint.0: Compare the dates and where the two sources were posted.
x-e-m1-07.s.s2.hint.1: Think about what the notice starting with 'Update:' tells you.
x-e-m1-07.s.s2.r.a: This judgment treats the printed one as more official. Compare the dates of the two sources and whether there is a reason.
x-e-m1-07.s.s2.r.b: This is a judgment that compared the dates and the sources of the two sources.
x-e-m1-07.s.s2.r.d: This judgment relies on a friend's words even though there is evidence you can check.
x-e-m1-07.s.s2.explain: The notice was posted two weeks after the poster by the same student council and even gives the reason for the change (Room 101 painting), so it is reasonable to follow it. However, the notice does not mention the price, so if you want to check, you can ask the student council.
x-e-m1-07.s.s3.prompt: Tell your friend Sora, who has seen only the poster, in one or two English sentences. The changed day and place must be included.
x-e-m1-07.s.s3.hint.0: First think about what information Sora knows from the poster.
x-e-m1-07.s.s3.hint.1: Write the two changes (the day and the place) in one sentence or split them into two sentences.
x-e-m1-07.s.s3.selfAssess.0: Did you tell both of the two things that changed?
x-e-m1-07.s.s3.selfAssess.1: Did you make clear that the poster's information is no longer correct?
x-e-m1-07.s.s3.selfAssess.2: Did you avoid saying again that the time is the same, when there was no need to?
x-e-m1-07.s.s3.modelNote.1: An answer that told it as an instruction for action.
x-e-m1-07.s.s2.r.c: That many people have seen it does not make the information correct. You need to compare the dates and where the two sources were posted.

x-e-m1-08.title: An email and a notice with different end times: making practice times that follow both
x-e-m1-08.goal: When two sources give different end times, recognize that you must follow both, and make several practice times that satisfy all the conditions.
x-e-m1-08.material:
You need to decide a club practice time. All the club students take the school bus on Wednesdays.

Source A: Email from the teacher in charge, Mr. Kim
"The club room is free on Wednesday from 3:30 p.m. to 5:30 p.m. The band uses the room until 3:30."

Source B: School notice
"The school bus leaves at 5:00 p.m. on Wednesdays. Students who take the bus must leave the club room by 4:45 p.m."

Write times as the number of minutes after 3 p.m. sharp, which counts as 0. Example: 3:30 = 30, 4:45 = 105.
x-e-m1-08.thinking.0: Satisfying the conditions of both sources at once
x-e-m1-08.thinking.1: Knowing that the stricter limit applies
x-e-m1-08.thinking.2: Making several answers and checking them
x-e-m1-08.prereq.0: Converting p.m. times into minutes and counting
x-e-m1-08.s.s1.prompt: The two sources give different end times (5:30 and 4:45). When all the club students take the bus, by what time must practice end?
x-e-m1-08.s.s1.hint.0: Write down who each source is talking to.
x-e-m1-08.s.s1.hint.1: Think about what would happen if you used the room until 5:30 and then tried to catch the bus.
x-e-m1-08.s.s1.r.a: This judgment picked the later time. Did you check whether Source B applies to these students?
x-e-m1-08.s.s1.r.b: This judgment picked the middle of the two times. Think about what kind of people each source is speaking to.
x-e-m1-08.s.s1.r.c: This judgment holds that both sources must be followed.
x-e-m1-08.s.s1.explain: The room is free until 5:30, but students who take the bus must be out by 4:45. Since all the students take the bus, following both means finishing at the earlier time, 4:45.
x-e-m1-08.s.s2.prompt: Make 3 different practice plans that follow both sources. The practice time should be at least 45 minutes and at most 60 minutes.
x-e-m1-08.s.s2.hint.0: The end time of practice (start + length) must be 105 or less.
x-e-m1-08.s.s2.hint.1: The start is 30 or more, after the band leaves. Since the length is fixed, change the start one by one.
x-e-m1-08.s.s2.ok.c1: You wrote it in whole minutes.
x-e-m1-08.s.s2.fail.c1: Write the start and the length in whole minutes.
x-e-m1-08.s.s2.ok.c2: It starts after 3:30, when the band leaves.
x-e-m1-08.s.s2.fail.c2: The band uses the room until 3:30. The start must be 30 or more.
x-e-m1-08.s.s2.ok.c3: It ends within the 5:30 set by the teacher.
x-e-m1-08.s.s2.ok.c4: It ends within 4:45 (105), when bus students must be out.
x-e-m1-08.s.s2.fail.c4: It goes past 4:45 (105), when bus students must leave the room.
x-e-m1-08.s.s2.ok.c5: The practice length is 45 to 60 minutes.
x-e-m1-08.s.s2.fail.c5: The practice length is at least 45 minutes and at most 60 minutes.
x-e-m1-08.s.s2.explain: The end time must be 105 (4:45) or less, and the start must be 30 or more. For example, start at 30 and practice for 45 or 60 minutes, or start at 45 and practice for 60 minutes. Starting at 60 and practicing 60 minutes ends at 120 (5:00), which goes past the bus students' limit, and starting at 0 overlaps with the band.
x-e-m1-08.s.s2.because.prompt: The end times of the two sources differ, but explain in one or two sentences why you fit it within 4:45 (105). You can write in Korean or English.
x-e-m1-08.s.s2.because.hint.0: Think about whether the two sources apply to the same students.
x-e-m1-08.s.s2.because.hint.1: Say which of 5:30 and 4:45 is the limit that must be followed first.
x-e-m1-08.s.s2.because.selfAssess.0: Did you say that both sources must be followed?
x-e-m1-08.s.s2.because.selfAssess.1: Did you say why the earlier time becomes the limit?
x-e-m1-08.s.s2.because.model.1: Since all the students take the bus, even though the room is free until 5:30, they have to be out by 4:45, so I made practice end within that time.

x-e-m1-09.title: Who is bringing the big paper? Fixing an ambiguous message
x-e-m1-09.goal: Find the line in a group message that can be read two ways, and rewrite it so it can be read only one way.
x-e-m1-09.material: This is a message that the group leader Ari posted in the class project group chat. The group members are Ari, Yuna, Mina and Juho, and they are trying to decide who will bring the big paper.
x-e-m1-09.thinking.0: Finding sentences that can be read two ways
x-e-m1-09.thinking.1: Understanding the cause of ambiguity (the pronoun she)
x-e-m1-09.thinking.2: Checking that the corrected sentence can be read only one way
x-e-m1-09.prereq.0: Easy words such as she, her, and told
x-e-m1-09.prereq.1: Experience working out which of the earlier people a pronoun refers to
x-e-m1-09.s.s1.prompt: Choose the line in the messages that, depending on the reader, can be read with two meanings.
x-e-m1-09.s.s1.hint.0: In each line, find the person that a word like 'he,' 'she,' or 'it' refers to.
x-e-m1-09.s.s1.hint.1: Check whether in any line the word can refer to two people.
x-e-m1-09.s.s1.explain: In line 2, 'she' could be Yuna or Ari. So it is not clear which of the two should bring the big paper. Lines 1, 3 and 4 can be read with the same meaning by anyone.
x-e-m1-09.s.s2.prompt: Rewrite line 2 in English so the person who brings the big paper can be read as only one person. Write it on the basis that Ari told Yuna to bring it.
x-e-m1-09.s.s2.hint.0: You can use a name or 'you' instead of 'she.'
x-e-m1-09.s.s2.hint.1: 'Big paper' must be in the sentence, and check that it is clear who the person is.
x-e-m1-09.s.s2.selfAssess.0: In your corrected sentence, can the person who brings the paper be read as only one person?
x-e-m1-09.s.s2.selfAssess.1: Does the meaning you decided on (Ari told Yuna to bring it) remain as it was?
x-e-m1-09.s.s2.modelNote.1: An answer that quoted the words directly so the person is clear.

x-e-m1-10.title: Writing a short email asking the teacher to change a test date
x-e-m1-10.goal: In an email with a purpose, a reader and a length limit, decide which information to include and leave out, and write it in English to meet the conditions.
x-e-m1-10.material: You have an English speaking test tomorrow (Friday), but you can't go because of a family schedule. You want to email your English teacher, Ms. Han, to ask to change the test date. Conditions: a polite email to a teacher, at least 25 words and at most 45 words.
x-e-m1-10.thinking.0: Choosing the necessary information within a limited length
x-e-m1-10.thinking.1: Choosing a tone that suits the reader (the teacher)
x-e-m1-10.thinking.2: Writing a request and an alternative together
x-e-m1-10.prereq.0: Polite email patterns such as Dear ..., and Could I ...?
x-e-m1-10.prereq.1: Reading and writing the names of the days of the week
x-e-m1-10.s.s1.prompt: Choose everything that must be in the email within 45 words.
x-e-m1-10.s.s1.hint.0: State the email's purpose in one sentence, and then check one by one whether each piece of information is needed for that purpose.
x-e-m1-10.s.s1.hint.1: Think about what the teacher needs to know in order to reply.
x-e-m1-10.s.s1.o.a: Writing the reason you can't come in one short sentence
x-e-m1-10.s.s1.r.a: Keeping the reason short helps politeness. Think about how much of the length limit the reason takes up.
x-e-m1-10.s.s1.o.b: Writing which test you can't take
x-e-m1-10.s.s1.r.b: The teacher reading it needs to know which test it is in order to change the schedule.
x-e-m1-10.s.s1.o.c: Easing the mood with a funny story
x-e-m1-10.s.s1.r.c: Think about the purpose of writing to a teacher and the length limit together.
x-e-m1-10.s.s1.o.d: Politely asking to change to another day
x-e-m1-10.s.s1.r.d: This choice states the purpose of the email clearly in a sentence.
x-e-m1-10.s.s1.o.e: Suggesting two days you could take the test
x-e-m1-10.s.s1.r.e: This choice gives an alternative so the teacher can decide right away.
x-e-m1-10.s.s1.o.f: Writing in detail from beginning to end what you did on the weekend
x-e-m1-10.s.s1.r.f: Within a length limit, writing information unrelated to the purpose can push out the information you need.
x-e-m1-10.s.s1.explain: The purpose of the email is a request to change the schedule, so which test it is, the request to change, and the days you are available are a must. A short reason is nice to have, but within the length limit it is optional.
x-e-m1-10.s.s1.acc.0: One short sentence of reason gives the teacher a polite impression. If it fits within the length limit, it is a good choice.
x-e-m1-10.s.s2.prompt: Write the body of the email to Ms. Han in English. Conditions: at least 25 words and at most 45 words, a polite tone, and include which test it is, the request to change it, and a suggestion of another day. If you write the sender's name at the end, it counts toward the word count.
x-e-m1-10.s.s2.hint.0: First write the greeting and which test it is in one sentence.
x-e-m1-10.s.s2.hint.1: Then suggest another day with a sentence like Could I take it on ...?, and count the words.
x-e-m1-10.s.s2.selfAssess.0: Did you keep to 25 to 45 words?
x-e-m1-10.s.s2.selfAssess.1: Are which test it is, the request to change, and another day all there?
x-e-m1-10.s.s2.selfAssess.2: Is the tone polite to a teacher?
x-e-m1-10.s.s2.modelNote.1: An answer that gave the reason briefly.
